findings.problem: The section teaches that the duties fall on the pharmacy 'rather than on its employees' and that employees and agents 'are reached through the seller's training and self-certification'; role_duties[2] gives an employee only the training point. That omits the provision that binds a seller's employees and agents directly: 21 U.S.C. 842(a)(14) makes it a prohibited act for 'a regulated seller or an employee or agent of such seller' to disclose logbook information in violation of the privacy regulations, or to refuse to provide the logbook to Federal, State, or local law enforcement authorities. It carries a civil penalty of up to $25,000 under 842(c)(1)(A), and a knowing violation can be prosecuted under 842(c)(2). The use restriction in 21 CFR 1314.45(b) is also not limited to the seller. Worked example [5] puts a store manager, who is an employee, in front of a local detective and concludes only that the entries 'may be disclosed ... as appropriate'. But 21 CFR 1314.45(a) says the information 'shall be disclosed as appropriate' to State and local law enforcement agencies, and refusing to provide the logbook is itself unlawful for both the seller and its employee.
findings.rationale: The duties in 21 CFR 1314.20-1314.42 are correctly placed on the regulated seller, and the definition of regulated seller does exclude employees and agents. But the section turns that definition into a statement about who is legally exposed, and there the statute says otherwise. A candidate would conclude that a Massachusetts pharmacist, intern, technician or clerk has no personal federal liability for leaking logbook entries or refusing a police request, and that giving a local detective the logbook is optional. The fix is short: add the 842(a)(14) prohibition on employees and agents, and describe disclosure to law enforcement as required 'as appropriate' rather than merely permitted. The exclusive wording in learning_objectives[0] ('rather than on its employees') also fails the overgeneralization criterion.

findings.problem: The section states the s. 4 conditions, the s. 5 conditions and record book, and the 21 CFR 1306.26 conditions exactly as the texts read. But orientation[0] lists a controlled-substance preparation among the products that 'can be sold in a Massachusetts pharmacy without a prescription'. The section never states the bottom line that its own verified premises lead to: no regulation under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 4 appears in 105 CMR 700.000, where 700.002 adopts 21 CFR 1308.11-1308.15 with no exception and the regulatory authority does not cite s. 4. None appears in 247 CMR 2.00-21.00 or in 105 CMR 720.000, 721.000, 722.000, 724.000 or 726.000 either. So no controlled-substance preparation can currently be sold under s. 5, and s. 17(c) requires a prescription. Instead the candidate is told to 'confirm that a s. 4 regulation actually excepts the preparation'. The section then builds a combined Massachusetts-and-federal sale in which 'both sets of conditions attach' (orientation[12], ma_vs_federal[1], decision_logic[10], common_traps[11]). That sale cannot arise under current law. Section 4(3) allows an exception only for a preparation 'similarly excepted' under the federal Act, and 21 U.S.C. 811(g)(3) exempts only (A) nonnarcotic preparations 'approved for prescription use', (B) preparations not for administration to humans or animals, and (C) certain anabolic steroid preparations. None of these is a nonprescription controlled substance to which 21 CFR 1306.26 applies, and no preparation containing a narcotic such as opium can be exempted for human use. Worked example [3] nevertheless supposes a s. 4 exception for a nonprescription opium-containing Schedule V preparation and resolves that 'for an adult the Massachusetts ceiling would limit the sale to four ounces in any 48 hour period'.
findings.rationale: The textual comparison in comparison_tables[2] and the s. 5 conditions that MA-Q-0121 tests are accurate and useful. The problem is how the route is framed for Massachusetts facts. A candidate is likely to remember 'Massachusetts: an adult may buy up to 4 oz of an OTC Schedule V opium or codeine preparation in 48 hours, subject to the federal age of 18'. That sale is not available in Massachusetts: no s. 4 exception exists, and s. 4(3) could not except such a preparation under current federal law. The section should add a dated statement that no s. 4 exception currently appears in the Department's or the Board's regulations, so the s. 5 route is not now available and a Schedule III-VI preparation needs a prescription. It should also qualify orientation[0], and either drop or clearly label as unavailable the combined-regime material and the adult four-ounce resolution of worked example [3]. For the same reason, study_usefulness_without_legal_distortion fails.

findings.rationale: This is an observation and does not by itself fail the criterion. 21 CFR 1314.100, cited first, contains both figures, so neither figure is unsupported and a candidate is not misled. Adding 830(d)(1) would make the statutory citation exact. Every other figure is attributed to text that contains it: 3.6 g to 1314.20(a) and 830(d)(1); the mobile vendor's 7.5 g to 1314.20(b) and 830(e)(1)(A)(ix)(II); 9 g, with its 7.5 g shipping limit, to 844(a) and not to 1314.20.

findings.problem: The paragraph lists that s. 27 states 'no prescription requirement, no minimum age, no identification requirement, no quantity limit and no record', then says 'That is the product of chapter 208 of the Acts of 2018'. Sections 47 and 48 of that act struck only the age-18 words and the proof-of-identification sentence. findings.rationale: This is an observation and does not by itself fail the criterion. The same sentence then describes exactly what the 2018 act struck, and every statement of current law is correct, so a candidate applying current Massachusetts law is not misled. results.summary: MINOR_EDIT, Medium. I checked the section's federal and Massachusetts content against current eCFR, the U.S. Code, malegislature.gov and mass.gov, and it is accurate throughout. Correct points include: the 3.6-gram calendar-day limit on every regulated seller; the 7.5-gram 30-day limits on mobile retail vendors (1314.20(b); 830(e)(1)(A)(ix)(II)) and on mail-order sellers that must report (1314.100); and the 9-gram 30-day figure placed on the purchaser under 844(a), which DEA's 2006 preamble also says is 'imposed on the purchaser, not the seller'. Also correct: blister packaging; behind-the-counter placement and direct delivery; the logbook, identification, signature methods, warning notice, two-year retention, central-record notice and privacy rules; the single 60 mg pseudoephedrine package exempted from both the logbook and identification (830(e)(1)(A)(iii)-(iv)); training, per-location self-certification, the 12-23 month grouping, annual renewal, and the $21 fee with its pharmacy waiver (1314.42(b)); 15-day loss reporting; and 1314.10. The statement that Massachusetts adds nothing is dated and limited to M.G.L. c. 94C, 247 CMR and 105 CMR 700.000, and it is accurate: a sweep of all 89 sections of c. 94C, every 247 CMR chapter and the 2024 edition of 105 CMR 700.000 found no such provision. The pseudoephedrine tracking bills S.1243 and H.1581 have not been enacted. The s. 4 and s. 5 conditions and record book, 21 CFR 1306.26 and 1304.04, s. 17(c), s. 27 as amended by St. 2018, c. 208, ss. 47-48, s. 32I(d), c. 111, s. 25K and the Board advisory all match their texts, and the advisory's recommendations are presented as guidance. All four practice questions (MA-Q-0107, 0108, 0114, 0121) are answerable from the section and not contradicted by it. There are two Medium defects. First, the section says the seller's employees are reached only through training, but 21 U.S.C. 842(a)(14) directly prohibits an employee or agent from disclosing logbook information unlawfully or refusing to provide the logbook to law enforcement, and worked example [5] softens 1314.45(a)'s 'shall be disclosed as appropriate' to 'may'. Second, the section presents the s. 5 excepted-preparation route, and a combined s. 5 and 1306.26 sale, as available without stating that no s. 4 exception currently exists. That combined sale cannot arise under 21 U.S.C. 811(g)(3), yet worked example [3] resolves that an adult could buy four ounces of an opium-containing Schedule V preparation. Two Low observations concern one partial statutory citation and a loose historical attribution of the 2018 act.
